title: Biomechanical Design, Additive Manufacturing, and Proof-of-Concept Evaluation of a 3D-Printed Transradial Prosthesis with a Manual Ratchet-Type Locking Mechanism
content: Background/Objectives: Upper-limb loss represents a critical clinical and socioeconomic challenge globally, causing significant functional limitations and psychological distress. This work presents the preliminary biomechanical design, Fused Deposition Modeling (FDM) manufacturing, and proof-of-concept mechanical evaluation of a customized transradial upper-limb prosthesis (Extremidad Variable y Adaptable, EVA) featuring a manual, incremental ratchet-type phalanx tensioning and locking mechanism. Methods: The virtual prosthesis assembly was modeled in SolidWorks and parametrically customized based on user anthropometric measurements. Finite element analysis (FEA) and numerical simulations in COMSOL Multiphysics were conducted to evaluate structural stresses, contact pressure, and stick-slip transitions under typical functional loads (up to 245 N) for three contact materials (wood, iron, and glass). Physical prototypes were manufactured in Polyethylene Terephthalate Glycol (PETG) and thermoplastic polyurethane (TPU) on a desktop FDM printer, followed by static load-bearing experiments to characterize mechanical performance and failure modes. Results: Mechanical simulations demonstrated that under the maximum design load, the peak equivalent Von Mises stress in the phalanges remains below the elastic limit of PETG (45 MPa vs. 47–60 MPa). COMSOL contact analysis and physical testing established safe grip thresholds without slippage of up to 5.3 kg for wood, 3.4 kg for iron, and 2.1 kg for glass. Physical static load-bearing tests confirmed structural integrity up to 5.0 kg; failure occurred at 7.5 kg due to fatigue-induced snapping of the internal spring rather than material fracture. Wear simulations modeled via Archard's law predicted a maximum wear depth of less than 0.05 mm on distal phalanges after 10⁴ cycles. Conclusions: This study validates the mechanical feasibility of the ratchet-type mechanical prosthesis. The design provides an accessible, structurally sound, and lightweight alternative for unilateral amputees. However, the manual mechanism imposes a functional limitation, requiring the use of the intact contralateral limb to engage and release grasp, thereby restricting complete bimanual independence. Future work will focus on integrating fingertip tactile sensors, performing cyclic fatigue testing, and conducting clinical validation with end users.
